review: I am old, like "I remember a time before FPS's existed" old. The older I get the more I can fool myself into thinking that I'm bad at modern shooters with their cover mechanics and regenerating Hit Points, but that I am a god of old-school, "proper" shooters like we had when I was young. Turns out that this was wrong, Amid Evil showed me that I just generally suck at video games. Thank you for removing the nostalgia-based cobwebs from my eyes, and for teaching an old man that though he has not always been old, he has always sucked at shooting things.

A homage to old school magic shooters like Heretic while possessing the soul of Quake, Amid Evil is a magnificent wizard warrior smack-down where you go from blighted realm to blighted realm cleansing them of evil...by force.  The enemies are varied and numerous, the weapons powerful and satisfying, and the maps are complex and littered with secrets to discover.  Much in the vein of the old build engine games, you can always find that extra powerful weapon a little early.

In my opinion, the best way to enjoy this game is Warrior Mode on Evil difficulty, meaning you always start with your powerful melee axe and nothing else.  It makes the magical weapons scattered about the levels more satisfying and impactful to find.  If you're an old school shooter veteran, Evil difficulty should be very doable and engaging.  You can quick save as often as you like or not at all.  The game auto saves whenever you get a major key during level progression, or you can go super hardcore and choose to restart the level if you die.

Compare this game to other great retro shooters like Dusk and Ion Fury and you'll get the idea of what you're in for.  There's even lore tidbits to read, although unlike the modern Doom games, you don't really have to work for them since most of it already exists in your codex.  Mostly just there for flavor.  Welcome for sure, but not the game's strong point.

The game's strong point is circle strafing, fast grabbing health and mana, and annihilating scores of enemies, most of which will run right at you hellbent on killing you.  If that's your sort of pleasure (and it certainly is mine), I highly recommend Amid Evil.
Thankfully, the difficulty selection room is really easy to navigate
At this point just play any new blood game that comes out because they'd be worth everypenny.

Your axe spins around and deals massive damage.
You can turn enemies into water with your basic weapon.
You have a sword that shoots green blades.
You have a trident that shocks enemies and melts them from the inside.
You can crucify enemies with crystals.
You have a stick that shrinks planets and makes you shoot them at your enemies.
Your BFG shoots a black hole.

Play this game.

+ Brutal fantasy boomer shooter inspired by games like Hexen and Heretic.
+ Great level design and environments puzzles. One of the levels in particular stands out and is just pure psychedelic imagination. 
+ Interesting and distinct zones.
+ Just the right length and doesn't overstay its welcome (so says yer mum) both for the zones and the whole game. 
+ RTX ray tracing puts a nice modern touch on the unfiltered textures and abstract environment. 

- Can't really say anything negative about game except that if you're not a fan of the genre you're not going to like it.

Side note: Don't know why they're called "boomer shooters" when these types of games were made by Gen X and played by Millennials. I distinctly recall Boomers being shocked by these types of video games.

Andrew Hulshult, once again, releases a great album. As usual, it comes with a game too. Pretty cool little bonus.

This game really reminded me of being a teen in the late 90s, during a time when it seemed like games were really trying to constantly introduce novel weapons. Maybe that's just me, and my experience, but that's what it feels like to remember those days. This game seems to want to do that. The trick is making the weapons functionally familiar, but different in all other ways. Sure, there's a "rocket launcher," but it's a claw that materializes a literal planet to hurl at your enemies. Yeah, there's a "shotgun," but it's a crystal mace that pins enemies to walls. Of course there's a BFG, but it's some sort of...arrangement of metallic ribbons that electrocutes enemies until they explode.

Definitely a cool game. Really bizarre levels, a few standout bosses, fun combat arenas. Definitely worth playing. If you like the demo, buy the game, because it's way more of that.

If you are an Old Human like me, then you played HEXEN and HERETIC which were probably the best of the third-party games that used the original id DOOM engine. This game is meant to invoke that experience, and does a fine job of it. The graphics are improved JUST enough that you don't go blind while still managing to give you the feel of the games it's riffing on. The cheesiness factor is high, on purpose.

But if you are NOT an Old Human, you still want to play this because it is a very good no-muss-no-fuss shooter. There are secret areas and insane weapons and bizarre scenery and a whole lot of run-n-gun fun. Also, there are cheats documented RIGHT THERE IN THE GAME so if you are like me and sometimes you just don't want to deal with the Boss of the Day the honest way, you're set.

The buzz around Amid EvilI set high expectations. A couple of levels later those expectations were already beaten by the sheer ingenuity, masterful craft and extraordinary execution of the team behind this masterpiece. This is such a trippy and challenging ride, it can easily fit into anybody's top ranked games in the genre kind of list.

If you consider yourself an FPS fan you MUST play this, please. It is a mind blowing experience that you will remember years down the line.

I did not expect this one to suck and fuck as hard as it did, but I walked away from getting all of the achievements feeling like I'd climbed into bed with a real pro and an unlimited card. Not the flashy, Michael Jordan of sex, but the reliable, unstoppable Wilt Chamberlain of sex. Which in retrospect may have also just been Wilt Chamberlain.

Every single gun in this game would be the best gun in another game. The soul mode is just icing on the cake. Every enemy gives a great, visceral feedback that only gets better on higher difficulty. The game never really crushed my balls per se, but the experience was really better for it. More of a light squeezing, some gentle almost foreplay CBT where a lot of other retro throwback shooters at times want to crush them like grapes. Not to say this game isn't hard, my pineal eye is just pretty adapted and open to this particular subgenre and once I understood exactly how the game was going to be it started to flow almost uninterrupted.

I should also say that of the three big retro throwback games (Ion Fury, Dusk, Amid Evil (Thanks Civvie)), I went into this one with the lowest expectations and came out with it being my favorite. Something about the art for me just doesn't really make sense when viewed without controlling it. When you're actually playing it, everything makes sense in a way that isn't immediately obvious.

Five stars out of five. Developers could sneeze into my open mouth and I'd thank them. Inject the DLC directly into my veins.

This summer I'm spending my spare time lifting and playing retro shooters,  IMHO this one is better than Dusk, the best game released by New Blood to date.

As strange as this may seem, the recent addition of RT fits like a glove with the outdated graphics and low resolution textures. 

They have done an amazing job with the level design, the game is perfectly balanced and full of rich settings. Every episode is a different universe on its own.

Amid Evil is a first-person shooter with a medieval theme by Indefatigable, which was founded by some of the developers behind the 2013 reboot of Rise of the Triad.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

Amid Evil’s gameplay is designed like an old-school FPS, where you play as a fast character that kills a lot of enemies per level.

There is no armor in the game, so your character is a bit squishier than in games like Doom or Quake. This means you’ll have to make sure you’re constantly moving because enemies can make mincemeat out of you quickly if you aren’t constantly on the move.

The gameplay also borrows a bit from the game Hexen. Like Hexen, weapons are magic-infused staves and medieval weapons that are powered by mana instead of ammo, down to having the same blue and green mana that Hexen had. The game adds two extra mana types, orange and purple for some variety. 

The game features seven weapons. Some of these are fairly typical FPS weapons with a medieval twist, while others are unorthodox in how they work. The Star of Torment is a mace that behaves like a shotgun, but shoots projectiles that pin enemies to the wall when killed, while the Voltrider is a fairly weak hitscan weapon that can cause dying enemies to explode if you keep hitting them with it as they die, causing electricity to spew out of the victim’s body and annihilate any living enemies near the victim.

The arsenal is well-balanced. Each weapon has its own purpose, and you’ll be finding new ways to use weapons as you proceed. For example, the Staff of the Azure Orb, the first ranged weapon you’ll get, is your best weapon against small flying enemies and enemies that like to dodge your attacks because it’s projectiles home in on enemies. This makes it very useful throughout the game instead of being the token crappy starter weapon. Even the game’s melee weapon, the axe, is useful due to how powerful it is. You’ll find yourself switching weapons often instead of relying on one or two obviously overpowered weapons throughout the entire game, making combat feel dynamic and fun throughout the entire game. It’s one of those games where you can tell a lot of care was put into making all of your weapons useful, and it shows.

The game also has powerful alt-fires for each weapon, like in Hexen, but they’re triggered differently. Instead of using a consumable item, they’re activated by collecting souls dropped from dead enemies and found in levels. Once your “soul meter” is at 100%, you can enable alt-fires for a limited time by hitting the alt-fire key.  The time you have alt-fires can be extended by collecting souls while you’re in alt-fire mode.

The alt-fire modes kick your weapons into overdrive. The Voltrider turns into a beam gun that melts the opposition, the Star of Torment shoots more projectiles that home in on enemies, and the game’s BFG9000 clone, the Aetherum, shoots black holes that can kill everything except bosses in one hit, but can also kill you if you’re too close to it.

These alt-fire modes are a great addition to the game. Besides being a blast to use, they’re also handy for getting out of a sticky situation. Since they can be used at any time once the soul meter is full, it might be tempting to conserve it until you absolutely need it, but levels have enough souls that you can go nuts with them. 

The only issue with the alt-fires is that the Axe and Staff of the Azure Orb have fairly underwhelming alt-fires that are either a fun but not the most practical gimmick (the axe) or made obsolete by another weapon’s alt-fire (the Staff of the Azure Orb). It’s not much of a problem though, since the other weapons have great alt-fires and you’ll always have a ranged weapon when you can activate alt-fire mode, so you’ll never need to depend on the axe’s alt-fire.

Each episode has its own enemies, which makes them play differently from each other. Enemies follow generic types, such as “big flying guy” or “small cannon fodder”, but they have just enough quirks per episode to make you change how you play. One episode might have dodge-happy enemies, while another will have lots of cannon fodder that’s small and surprisingly fast, forcing you to use a weapon in a way you weren’t expecting, then the next episode will make you focus more on taking down mini-bosses with powerful weapons. It adds a lot of variety to episodes.

[h1]Levels[/h1]

The game is broken down into seven episodes with four levels each, with the last level being a dedicated boss level. There is also a secret gag level and a standalone bonus level that’s meant to show off RTX lighting.  Completing each episode will strip you of every weapon except the axe.

Make no mistake; this game’s levels are gorgeous. They might look pixely and a little ugly in images, but it’s completely different in motion. The colors are vivid and there’s a lot of unique architecture (particularly in later episodes) that’ll make you say “wow!” when you see it. The episodes Arcane Expanse and The Abyss in particular are a perfect blend of great color usage and amazing architecture. Even the skyboxes are great, mixing realistic skies with old-school looking mountains that perfectly nail the look of how old skyboxes. You’ll find RTX lighting makes levels look even better, so turn it on if your GPU can support it.

The unique architecture isn’t just for show; you’ll often find yourself walking or jumping through it. This means you’ll occasionally be fighting enemies on tight but spiraling paths or unusual architecture, so the cool-looking architecture provides for fun and unique challenges instead of merely being eye candy. It’s great to see a developer use cool-looking architecture for gameplay instead of being merely background props.

Levels are large, except for boss stages. You’ll likely spend around 15 minutes for levels in your first playthrough, so there’s plenty of meat in each episode despite them being “only” four levels each. This gives episodes great pacing; there’s enough content in each episode to make it a satisfying romp, but they never overextend their stay.

The actual level design itself is straightforward. Where you’re supposed to go is clearly laid out and levels are chunked in a way that you’re not going to have to do things like backtrack all the way back to a small and obscure area at the start of a map after getting a key on the opposite side of the level.

There is a bit of platforming in this game, but it’s fine for the most part since your character has good air control and platforms are wide enough that there’s plenty of space to land on. There are two episodes where the platforming segments might give someone trouble: the heavy amount of platforming in The Forge and the water bubbles in the Arcane Expanse, which have unusual mechanics that’ll take some time bit to get used to.

The worst levels are in The Forge. The Forge’s level design puts too much emphasis on annoying traps and jumping around, which gets grating after a while. There’s a bit of platforming in other episodes, sure, but The Forge combines a lot of platforming segments with traps that just get on your nerves after a while, like having to run between gears that can crush you, ride gears up and hop between them to get somewhere, or hit switches, avoid spikes, and jump on platforms before the platforms retract, forcing you to do the whole thing over. Lots of platforming and traps in one episode just doesn’t work together in an FPS. At least the enemies are fun and challenging.

[h1]Final thoughts[/h1]

Amid Evil is a very well-made FPS that combines a great weapon set, a diverse cast of enemies, and amazing levels to create a fantastic experience. It draws influence from old FPS games, such as Hexen and Unreal 1, but stands on its own as a unique experience instead of being a mere copy of 90s FPS games. It’s highly recommended for any fans of FPS games or for gamers that want a feast for the eyes.

Alright game, play fun.

...With one huge caveat though: your computer must be strong enough to run modern AAA at "high", since this game is also quite demanding on the hardware — don't look at its "boomer shooter" artistic style, it's a proper high-end Unreal Engine 4 title. On its low settings, the game becomes barely playable: even if the combination of low resolution with bad aliasing won't literally make your eyes bleed, then the very next minute you'll discover enemies attacking you from beyond their drawing distance. If you can't run Amid Evil on "high" — I'd rather recommend you put it off until you can. I don't think this game will disappear anytime within the next decade or two; even if somehow it gets delisted from Steam, you should still be able to find it in other places.

Once you have a machine beefy enough to run Crysis 2 — then for all means, give this game a try!

A gorgeous but tedious FPS. There are no problems or flaws with any element of Amid Evil. The problem that it doesn't have nearly enough to be interesting.

There is no alt.fire on weapons and little variety in actual gample application of weapons (no grenade launcher type weapon, no reason to use melee weapon, no weapon with a knockback to get melee enemies off of you), no weapon combos due to very slow weapon swap speed, no active items, barely any powerups (I found "Invisibility" in a secret area once), no interactive objects on the map (explosive barrels e.t.c.), no movement options like slide, dash, double jump e.t.c  (to the naked eye even strafe jumping isn't faster than normal jumping). All you can do is choose from 5 stunningly looking and sounding weapons, hold down Left MB and circle around the arena. 

You have 2 "super abilities":  BFG weapon and "soul something mode" which turns any weapon you're holding into even deadlier tool of destruction than BFG. But you never fight more than 5-10 enemies at once; levels can have 15-30 small encounters stretched across kilometers of amazing architecture and interioirs. 

For some reason Amid Evil is deelpy afraid of giving the player an experience of a big scale battle. Maybe it has something to do with the fact that most enemies run faster than the player, can leap, charge, fly or even dodge roll attacks, while the player controls a boring turret.

Just having the player run fast and not having chest-high walls in level design isn't enougn to craft good FPS gameplay. After 3 episodes on "Evil" difficulty I found myself having to talk myself into launching the game with a hope of having fun. So I decided not to.

This is one of the best run and gun FPS games ever made. I'm kicking myself for not getting it sooner.  
Not only is the game play fun and varied, the audio and visuals are at absolute maximum quality for the game type. This game was a labor of love by people that worked towards executing a vision of near perfection.

"How do we make our rocket launcher stand out from all the other rocket launchers in all the other shooters?"

"What if it's not a rocket launcher, but a wand that teleports planets from elsewhere in the universe, shrinks them down to the size of a football, and hurls them at your enemies?"

- A conversation at Indefatigable Games, probably

Just about everything you could want from this kind of retro FPS. Unique, memorable, magical, and sprawling environments that are packed with secrets. Varied level design that's full of twists and turns but rarely difficult or annoying to navigate. Fast-paced gameplay that demands the player never stop moving. Brilliant weapons, some of which are really fresh and interesting, others that don't really deviate from the standard FPS fare in terms of pure mechanics, but stand out thanks to beautiful designs and deeply satisfying animations and sounds (did I mention the wand that launches planets?). Even the basic melee weapon is powerful and fun to use. A mix of old school and modern graphical trappings that lends the game a totally unique visual style. Moody, atmospheric soundtrack. 

Only negatives is most of the bosses felt pretty lacklustre, and outside of the final episode, I didn't find Amid Evil quite as challenging as the games that inspired it, or its contemporaries in this little retro shooter revival we're having (though I was playing on hard; there is a secret "Evil" difficulty for players that really want to punish themselves). These are minor issues with an otherwise thoroughly fun experience, though. 

Tasty little game. Go play it.

A fantastic FPS boomer shooter that has some really nice designs and weapons for the game. The combat system is also pretty well done, and the levels are pretty well designed as well. The enemies are also perfect, especially for the level's theme. 

Definitely one of my favorite FPS of all time, and would recommend it to anyone.

TL;DR - AMID EVIL if retro-FPS porn. Recommended is not the word.

Dear ID software, let me tell you a story.

I remember when I first played the original Quake. I was blown away by the 3D space, the bizarre architecture, the subdued colours, vicious enemies, overwhelming atmosphere, unnerving music, everything. I was in heaven and wanted more.

Then Quake 2 came out and it was some alien BS, completely unrelated to source material. After that, Quake 3 -  a great multiplayer game, but not much more. Quake 4 was a cartoonish reboot of Quake 2 with cinematics and a hovercraft section that was as enjoyable as d!ck-flavoured toothpaste. By the time I killed the Strogg leader for the second time, I was ready to gauge my eyes out with a blunt d!ldo.

With each subsequent instalment my hope of ever seeing a sequel to the original Quake 1, with all its grim charm, Lovecraftian beasts, unique surroundings and that unforgettable roughness of the hostile world, died a little. But it still lingered, it was still there somewhere.

Then Quake Champions came out. And whatever remained of my hope died a horrible, gruesome death.

I shrugged my shoulders and thought to myself: "Guess it's time to move on". And so I strolled away towards the land of countless Q1 ports and the such, until I came across AMID EVIL.

This game is everything Quake 1 could have been and should have been, and more. It's like a sequel to Q1, and Heretic, and Hexen, and it does not disappoint. It's got the right atmosphere, the right mechanics, the right enemies, weapons, level design, architecture, textures etc. - it's got all this and so much more. It's like a breath of fresh air, without the stench of cinematics and other modern crap that literally nobody asked for.

The wait is over. My dream came true, my prayers have been answered. The true successor to Quake 1 is here, and its name is AMID EVIL.

So yeah, you can keep churning out another Strogg adventure after another, you can implement RTX support all you want, you can even add a battle-royale mode, a mariachi band, a line of cocaine and a free hooker with every new game - I don't f***ing care. You failed me, ID. You failed to do a decent sequel to Quake 1. And somebody else had to do it for you. And they did.

Yours sincerely,
- the fans.

Being a fan of both Quake and Heretic/Hexen the spark didn't really jump with this one. It is well designed on one hand but on the other it's also terribly boring. There isn't the grittiness of a Quake nor a dark, fantasy vibe as in Heretic/Hexen either.

If you are nit-picky like me, enjoy the read.

This game just frustrates me and ends up being more of a chore to finish than fun; and not for difficulty, it's tedious.
Hopefully something the devs can use a negative view of the game, maybe some some ideas of stuff to polish up.

I played through on normal(warrior mode, auto soul mode) and hard(warrior mode, auto soul mode, no HUD).

Level Design:
Level where rotating blocks hurt you even when moving away from you.
Blue water effect not triggering in water sometimes.
Elevators not activating when moving on them, have to re-trigger it.
Annoying use of elevator traps in front of weapons that drop you down when trying to grab it. Used SEVERAL times, way overstayed its welcome.
Enemies spaced apart just so as to make you waste most of your soul power-up almost every time. This problem also gives levels an almost predictable tempo of around 2-4 enemies every corner passed.
Item spacing is just a bad; tons of mana everywhere, then for mind boggling reasons a full mana pick up within like 10 steps from several normal pick-ups of the same color. Same with full soul power-up, and multiple full healths on levels with tons of small healths.
Level secrets seem to often make me not even want to look. They would often end up a few ways: sitting in plain sight, slightly under something or over a shallow hill, a similar spot with just nothing in it, a temping spot blocked by an invisible wall, or a slightly hidden spot with stuff in it, but not a secret. Even in warrior mode secrets are mostly irrelevant for getting every weapon every stage.
Jumping out of water feels sloppy and often get caught on the surface.
For some unintelligible reason, many MANY of the games torch sconces/baziers are so low that you can walk right over them without getting stopped, and yes, it hurts you.
Level hazards aren't consistent, some hurt you, some out right kill you.
Lava hurts you more than once if you jump.

Enemies:
Some enemies are as fast as you, obviously you could shoot them, but if you didn't they would just stay glued to you attacking.
Unreliable flinching: shoot them 5 times, get 2 flinches. Shoot them 8 more times, get no flinches. Hit a guy with the beefy axe 4 times, no flinch.
Enemies are too tanky which makes the unreliable flinching worse. Lower enemy health or preferably better balance the weapons.
Enemies fire through each other which can lead to impossible to dodge obscured bullets.
Slow start up animations and then fast projectiles.
"Better AI than doom", yet enemies with limited range(bomb throwers, snakes) shoot at any distance, even with no chance of hitting you. Flying enemy description says they never go melee range, but can easily be led to do just that.
Some animations are bad or non existent. Exploding arm shooting enemy's limb just reappear instantly after shooting them.
Mediocre bosses normally, but also extremely exploitable. The obvious: get soul power, use mace, win. Some of the bosses were pretty good though.
Fish enemies can hit you while they are still in the water and you are on land.

Weapons:
The axe punishes you for using it. Using it against enemies close to you, the projectile speed is undodgable and doesn't interrupt enemy attack animations. It loses the enemy pulling ability when powered up, you can often get heavily punished using it powered up which is cool. (it could get projectile blocking or life steal to actually feel good empowered.
Awkward start up on every weapon, some I get, but the wand and trident make no sense. Claw does not have startup lag.
For as heavy and slow firing as the sword is, the power doesn't translate. And functionally it doesn't make sense, edges pierce and are weak, but the middle is more power but doesn't pierce. So practically the same damage unless you pierce SEVERAL enemies. For a skill shot medium speed projectile weapon it just isn't rewarding when you could just spam homing wand and do way better. My suggestion would be extra damage for distance traveled, or just always pierce. This weapon feels amazing powered up.
The wand just takes no skill and can do very comparable damage to every weapon except the last few.
Trident isn't worth the effort going for overcharge most the time with how easy it is to fail. Like the sword, just use wand and save yourself the trouble.
The two weapons I found the most fun were the axe and claw because they actually take enemies out quickly. The claw has no startup lag and actually pretty ridiculous fire rate. The axe unfortunately feel like they don't want you to enjoy using it for the previously stated reasons. Still more fun getting punished using the axe than using pea shooter spam.
The claw soul mode is totally counter intuitive, even bad.(shakes the screen horribly) Has a huge explosion, big shock wave, all that screen shake, and as far as I could tell no extra radius, only damage. But still can't even kill a claw wizard in one hit.
BFG seemly doesn't see enemies close to the detonation for seeming no reason. Not with too many enemies even with just a few. Maybe the enemies body block each other from getting hit by it, negating part of its whole point of being a group attack.
If you run out of mana, it switches back to the axe automatically, and if you try to select the empty weapon it will switch back and forth from axe to current weapon.

Power-ups:
Souls: can still be picked up even on a full charge. Either make them not pick up or give small health bonus(that goes over 100). This was a problem even playing on auto soul mode.
Torch- way too short, considering it gives the player no actual power gain.
Flight- also way too short, you have to know where you want to go before even getting it. Can't actively explore with it.
Invisibility- great until you hit an enemy and not kill it, then they just start attacking you like normal. Phony description of how invisibility works in the codex.
Invincibility works as intended, and has a good duration.
Mana boost not in the codex even though it uses the picture.
Some sentences not capitalized in the codex.

Player control:
Pointless crouch: Barely move down, no use for it in combat dodging, only use it sometimes to find secrets and a spinning axe on one level.
Too much momentum when slowing down while running and jumping. For as much platforming and catwalk navigating(while fighting) the movement control feels sloppy.

Amid Evil is a retro inspired, single player focused First Person Shooter, which has fast paced combat and is set in a world of magic.

The best part of Amid Evil is the unique weapons that are really fun to use. There’s a staff that shoots blue bolts which home in on enemies, a sword which fires arcs of green energy, a trident which fires lightning bolts from its prongs, a staff that fires miniature planets which explode on impact like RPGs, a spiked mace which fires its spikes like shrapnel, and a relic that creates an energy blast which destroys all nearby enemies like Doom’s BFG.

The other main gameplay mechanic allows you to collect the souls of defeated enemies and use them to activate “soul mode”, where your weapons have a more powerful alternate fire mode such as rapid fire, increased damage, or larger explosion radius, which is really useful for clearing large groups of enemies.

There’s a wide variety of enemies, including cultists, elementals, robots and demons. There’s a mixture of enemies who want to attack with melee and projectiles, and many have special abilities like a shield which reflects your attacks back at you, pouncing at you from long distances, flying, riding a demonic mount, teleportation, and more. And each chapter ends with a fight against a massive boss.

Level design is fantastic, old school mazes where you need to press switches to activate moving platforms and find keys to open locked doors, and featuring portals, underwater passages, spike traps, lava/acid pits, pools of water on the ceiling and impossible staircases. Each chapter has a different theme, from gothic architecture to Egyptian and a strange hell dimension. One chapter has a few too many jumping puzzles suspended over instant death bottomless pits for my liking, but the other six chapters were really enjoyable.

Hard difficulty is perfectly balanced to challenge a veteran FPS player without being frustrating. Controls are fully rebindable and work great with mouse and keyboard. I didn’t suffer from any bugs or crashes. It took me just under 9 hours to finish the game, but its cheap so you’ll get value for money at full price.

Amid Evil is a must play for all FPS fans.

AMID EVIL is a first person shooter coming to us from New Blood Interactive, made by the thrice blessed Indefatigable. Now let me set the record straight right off the bat. Despite what you might think, this isn't some throwback retro FPS game, oh no. This is an evolution.

AMID EVIL is a spiritual successor to Heretic, Hexen and Hexen 2 just like DUSK is the spiritual successor of DOOM, QUAKE and BLOOD. It hits you home with its myriad of spectacularly designed levels, the awesome variety of weapons and it's smoother than life controls within the first 15 minutes.

And let me tell you, you haven't even scratched the surface yet.

The game is divided into 7 episodes, each unique in its design, enemies and environments. From medieval moon worshiping cults, to giant stone guardians, to sentient machines and crystalline arcane constructs. You're going on a journey, player and you better come prepared.

Let's talk a little about the game-play, you're The Champion, you've claimed the Axe of the Black Labyrinth and you're ready to use it to bring order to chaos, life to death, but mostly, to destroy evil like the cosmic crusader you are.

The controls are tight and responsive in the most literal way. You don't feel like you're in control, you are in control, it's all muscle memory from here because the game doesn't play around. You'll be dodging and weaving and platforming like you were born to do it, because that's how much control you have over your character. The game doesn't hamstring you and doesn't dictate your route for you. It gives you absolute freedom. I've skipped whole sections by using old-school quake techniques like rocket (or planet) jumping, or just figuring out inventive ways to use the scenery to my advantage.

You've got 7 weapons to choose from and I'll put it right out there, there are no "good weapons" or "bad weapons". Each weapon has their use, has enemies that it is much better against. Fighting fire spirits? Use the water rod. Fighting projectile reflecting crusaders? Use the planet-tosser. Fighting incarnations of evil? Well, you got an axe made just for that don't you?

Each weapon has a unique firing mechanism and unlike most shooters, they don't stand to imitate the classic gun, shotgun, rocket launcher. Instead, you got a sword that fires shockwaves, a rod that fires homing shots, a lightning shooting trident, a planet tossing claw (yeah, it shrinks planets and throws them at enemies, try not to blow up the earth will you?), a mace that shoots crystal spikes and of course, cosmic ribbon candy of death. You're going to be switching weapons on the fly constantly, within the same fight, you're going to be strategizing, prioritizing and you're going to do it without even noticing, because it's just a pleasure to do.

I have to put a shout out to my man Andrew Hulshult for being the absolute master of FPS soundtracks and making the experience ten times better with his incredible tracks. I don't buy game soundtracks a lot, unless it's a bundle. But I went out of my way to buy this one, so I can listen to it everywhere. It's that good. I can't even describe it, just play the game and have a listen.

The environments and level design are probably the pinnacle of their kind for this sort of game. I spent over 30 minutes every level just exploring and taking it in. The sky boxes, the maps, the environment, hunting for secrets, just getting into every nook and cranny, not because there's an achievement for that, but because it was just so well made.

Though the game follows the John Carmack creed of plot design keeping it simple, there's a deceptive amount of lore in the game, given to the player through short messages hidden in each level. Such as rivalry between two factions of enemies you fight, or connection between episodes that you can see by exploring. It was more than enough for me, gave me more time to focus on the action and rewarded me for looking around where I could. (And yes Dave, I bought DUSK, thank you.)

The second way they convey this to you is with a very helpful codex right in your menu, giving you info about places and enemies you'll encounter, which I can say was very helpful to me starting out and helped get me into the game. Kudos for that!

All in all, like I said, this isn't a throwback, it's an evolution. I'm excited to see what more can be done with this genre now, New Blood and their partners are giving me newfound faith in the gaming industry.

But, nothing's perfect and I do need to mention some drawbacks to the game.

1. Clipping issues when flying and jumping. I've gotten stuck on a ledge more than once, kind of a bummer. If you guys fix that, that'll be great.

2. This game NEEDS a map editor!

3. Bosses were too easy for me. Granted, I'm a veteran of FPS's and I've been finding EVIL difficulty easy, but still.

I hope to see more from New Blood and Indefatigable in the future!

Amid evil is a game that looks pretty and does as little as possible. To get the praise out of the way, it is a very pretty looking game. It is the most triple A looking retro game I've ever seen, enviroments are pretty, enemies are pretty, weapons are pretty, soundtrack is alright.

The problem is that the game was designed by 3 seperate teams that evidently never communicated with one another. The maps, the enemies and the actual gameplay design in this game is completely discombombobulated resulting in a frustrating experience that never manages to click.

(For reference I beat the game on hard)

The main 3 issues that are the source of all the problems:

1.)  Enemies are bullet sponges. MASSIVE fucking bullet sponges. They eat an enormous ammount of damage, often comical ammounts of it. It can take upto 5-10 seconds of sustained fire to kill some enemies. There's no weapon combos or weapon swap techs for taking down enemies fast. The only way to kill enemies is to look at them for 10 seconds straight with your weapon of choice. Also, while the enemies have visual variety, they have ZERO gameplay variety. Play serious sam, ultrakill or doom, and you will have ever enemy attack pattern memorized by the time you beat them. All enemies are here are "generic projectile vomit" or "generic melee run at you". 

2.) Maps often place you in tiny arenas, narrow hallways, narrow bridges with no room to dodge or strafe and if you step off them you fall into the void and die instantly. Compounding this issue. Enemies spam a lot. They fire A LOT of projectiles, run super fast, and attack super often.

3.) You don't have a parry, you don't have a double jump, you don't have a dash. You can't even strafe because the maps are not designed for it. You don't have anything. All you can do is walk at a brisp pace. You don't have any mobility or any response to enemies other than looking at them and hoping they run out of health before they reach you or you run out of ammo. Your weapons also have no mechanics. They all do the same thing "Damage in XYZ shape." There's no "Shotgun for kleers, Sniper for biomechs, rocket launcher for bulls", rock paper scissors strategy that games like serious sam have.

And this is what completely kills the game. 

The maps are designed for ultrakill, except you don't have any of V1's mobility to navigate around enemies in confined spaces properly.  

The enemies are designed for serious sam, except you don't have the space required to properly circle strafe them and focus on dodging because maps are tiny and have instakill gaps everywhere.

Gameplay is designed for fucking doom 1995, except somehow worse. I am not joking when I say that the gameplay here feels like a placeholder. The weapons all suck. They have no punch, no kick, do no damage and aren't satisfying to use, with the maybe exception of the mace. There's no rock paper scissors matching game for weapons to enemies. All weapons just do generic damage in a generic area of effect in a different shape. You use a weapon until you run out of ammo and then swap to the next one.

This game gets a huge pass because its graphics are pretty. Strip away the graphics and there's nothing underneath. Absolutely skip. If you want a classic boomer shooter just buy dusk. Its the same thing but better.

AMID EVIL at its core is a wonderfully rendered retro throwback FPS that beckons the nostalgic memories of games such as Heretic and Hexen and Quake with gorgeous environments, beautiful weapon feel and a majestic combat encounters.

However, I come to you today not focused on the weapons, the enemies or the aesthetics, but rather something truly gorgeous: the Difficulty Selection level.

Most games dare not be so bold with something so seemingly obtuse as a Difficulty Selection level where it is not as simple as clicking a rather comedic naming on a menu. AMID EVIL, in this regard, dares to be different. There have been other reviews left for this game with scathing remarks as to the "poor design" of the Difficulty Selection. I disagree wholeheartedly. For you see, the Difficulty Selection tutorializes the player of the movement mechanics and the weight of the Champion in such an elegant and silent way that most take for granted. To go for the Easy difficulty, it is straightforward and one could get by the challenge by only holding the "W" key on the Keyboard. This is Leon Zawada and Simon Rance's brilliance coming into full display here. By having the Easy difficulty being so easy to access, it makes clear of the very nature of the room so as to not to cause further confusion with regards to the other options.

The Medium Difficulty is when the ingenuity of NewBlood Interactive shines however. To access the Medium Difficulty Portal, one must familiarize themselves with the Champion's capability of jumping. This is a quintessential part of AMID EVIL's movement. You are not as agile as the other NewBlood FPS stars like Duskdude (from DUSK) or V1 (from ULTRAKILL). You have to be more methodical with your movement, much slower, yet still a very crucial element to your survival. To fall down into the Medium Difficulty Pit, it taunts you with the question of "Perhaps this is not your destined path?". To fail a jump so quickly and to be absconded so humiliatingly gives a feeling to overcome a challenge after how insultingly easy it is to access the Easy Difficulty. Thus, it encourages more experimentation with AMID EVIL's jumping, and I find that riverting.

The Hard Difficulty being accessible through more timing-based platforming is definitely an eye-opener. AMID EVIL has some platforming trickeries (Many veterans of this game recall the torture that is E5M2 and E5M3 with regards to platforming) and it wants to hammer in the brutality of it early. While not all of AMID EVIL's levels feature extensive amounts of platforming, the sheer scale of the levels as well as the high enemy counts makes the levels feel expansive and massive. In a quiet bout of technical mastery, Indefatigable makes you wait to access the moving platforms for Hard Difficulty. This gives the player a pause to wait for the platforms, training their in-game rhythm but more pressingly, giving a moment of brevity to immerse yourself in the environment. AMID EVIL's environments are some of the most gorgeous I have ever seen in Video Games, and its RTX-On chunkiness means that it provides a unique graphical flavor I have yet to see replicated elsewhere as perfectly. AMID EVIL is a beautiful game, and to purposely include a moment of waiting makes accessing the Hard Difficulty that much sweeter.

Finally, we get to the EVIL Difficulty selection. It's hidden on the route to the Hard Difficulty. Even still, attention and exploration minds will discover this portal after a bit of trial and error. This, personally, is what makes AMID EVIL a 10/10 game for me. It rewards exploration with a fittingly difficult challenge (Although I did mostly get through AMID EVIL on my first playthrough on EVIL Difficulty). What's brilliant about this decision to hide the EVIL Difficulty is that AMID EVIL's levels, all 28 of them, rewards exploration in the form of secrets. Secrets can give the Champion access to Mana and Power-Ups to make your fights more nuanced and interesting, as well as some very funny easter eggs such as the... well, THE Fish. In this short bit, the player is made perfectly aware of the design intention of AMID EVIL, where your initiative to explore the levels, both in progression and in secret-hunting, is thoroughly awarded. Indeed, in the campaign itself, AMID EVIL has this beautiful pacing and choice of landmarks that makes every combat encounter simply unforgettable. AMID EVIL is breathtaking and quite frankly it is amazing that something as simple as a Difficulty Selection level can demonstrate its talents perfectly.

Also you do funny scream when you fall and die in the Difficulty Selection level.

You even get an achievement.

Buy now.

Amid Evil’s retro aesthetic disguises a surprisingly complex and technologically accomplished title. Running on Unreal Engine 4, complete with modern features including DX12 and Raytracing, this cutting edge tech works in combination with creative level design and environments to create a shooter which is not afraid to separate itself from typical throwback shooters.

Marketed as a ‘boomer shooter’ inspired by 1994’s Heretic, I didn’t expect Amid Evil to be so impressive in its presentation. The lighting and weather effects on levels such as ‘The Forges’, set in a decrepit Aztec ruin half-absorbed by marshland, features reflective rain-soaked surfaces which shine different colours in response to the type of magic you use. You can illuminate dark corridors, deep water caverns, or misty open areas using your spells and it all looks fantastically rendered. The grass in Amid Evil is somehow both 2D and the thickest, lushest grass I’ve seen in a long time. Performance was exceptional too, running at 60FPS during all but the most large scale encounters, and that’s a rather dated gaming laptop too (GTX 1650M, 8GB RAM).

The level design is equally impressive. Secrets are creatively hidden along cliff-faces or through secret switches that reward observation, and the game helpfully informs you to look up frequently – a slightly unassuming piece of advice which pays dividends. And these secret areas are worth finding too because the game, at times, can ramp up the difficulty. While the enemies are no slouch, and will often zigzag towards you instead of directly beelining, you’re often forced to platform while simultaneously being attacked. This can sometimes lean into frustrating territory, especially on the final episode where enemies begin seriously sponging your attacks, but in more sensibly built areas it can create an added life-or-death tension.

With the exception of the axe, which utilises a familiar stabby-stab function, the weapons of Amid Evil aim to be as varied as possible without being overly situational. Almost every weapon can be used in any encounter, but learning the enemies in detail will help you optimise your runs and pick the best weapon for the job. When you collect enough souls (mostly granted through kills) you’re given the option to enter an alt-mode which gives all your weapons a different and much, much more powerful mode which is heaps of fun to explore. My favourite was, once again, the axe which now spins in your hand and both rips through enemies or launches you through water like a speedboat.

I didn’t care much for the lore or setting really. While visually impressive, most of the lore is given through cryptic writing on walls which, unless you’re really dedicated to piecing together codex entries, just went in one ear and out the other. Strange complain here I’ll admit, but Amid Evil’s font is also really hard to read at times. This is just an annoyance on menus, but in-game it can be difficult to read your health bar at times.

Overall Amid Evil is a technically accomplished, satisfying and creative shooter which earns a standout place [A]midst a swarm of throwback retro shooters.

[h1]AMID EVIL[/h1]

This game spent over 2 years rotting in my library, and I will regret that for the rest of my life.

By far one of the coolest games I've played recently, this is an exceptionally perfect game with an 8 hour campaign and a bunch of other side content. To put it simply really, this game is like DOOM with fantasy, and magic elements mixed into it.

You could also literally run it on anything I'm sure.

New Blood never fails to create a brilliant modern retro experience.

[h2]10/10[/h2]

[b][i]AMID EVIL[/i] is very much [i]Quake[/i] 1 level design in a [i]Hexen[/i]/[i]Heretic[/i] universe.[/b] It's well done. We're a bit spoiled this year with outstanding '90s FPS shooters. Personally, I prefer both [i]Ion Maiden[/i] and [i]DUSK[/i] over this title for the following reasons:

1) I find [i]AMID EVIL[/i] to be a bit generic in terms of theme; the fantasy setting could use a bit more to set it apart.

2) I prefer real or low fantasy weapons/guns over wands and totally high fantasy weapons. Now, don't get it twisted - I appreciate that these high fantasy weapons exist, but yeah, they leave something to be desired. I miss reloading and all of that. 

3) The level design in [i]AMID EVIL[/i] is much more 'sprawling' (for lack of a better term) just like the original [i]Quake[/i]. Most levels are indoors in what feels like an underground compound (at the time of writing this review). I personally like the backwoods feel of [i]DUSK[/i], or the dystopian cityscape of [i]Ion Maiden[/i] far more. I want to look up at the sky in most levels.

4) The enemy design is different than the other two games I mention, which is good - but they all mostly have a 'same' kind of feel. The enemies are all super fast, so most of your efforts are focused on running backwards while fending them off. It's fun, but gunplay isn't quite as fun as the other two games for this particular reason.

5) The font and overall menu system definitely feels 'Early Access'. I know the font is being worked on, which is desperately needed. 

6) My favorite way to play the game is Endless mode - and I feel like that's a flaw in itself. It's the opposite for me with [i]DUSK[/i]. I want to fall in love with the campaign, but eh, there isn't really any story or anything all that interesting to suck me in. The secrets are super easy to find compared to the other two games, too.

7) No multiplayer. Now, I really don't care about this - but who designs a game in this genre without building this in from the ground up? You know the community is going to whine about this. Questionable design decision to say the least.

[b]Well, it sounds like I just dumped all over the game.[/b] Please don't get me wrong. [i]AMID EVIL[/i] is a welcome addition to the genre. The *great news* is that this is not just some reskin of [i]DUSK[/i] - it certainly is it's own thing. And that's really important. 

[b]Pros:[/b]
+Fairly polished game for Early Access
+It's the most modern version of the original [i]Quake[/i] we've seen this year
+Well optimized
+Lots of content right now

[b]Cons:[/b]
-The universe is generic
-No multiplayer
-The font is too hard to read
-Music is nothing to write home about
-The secrets are easy, and there really aren't all that many of them
-Weapons could use more 'oomph' to them; also we should be able to use the special ability when we want to as opposed to it autotriggering

[b]I was psyched out of my mind for [i]AMID EVIL[/i] - and while it is certainly good - I think I'll be focused more on [i]DUSK[/i] and [i]Ion Maiden[/i].[/b] Because, let's face it, gaming time is valuable and we can't play everything.

So yeah, it's another low-key game which puts AAA studios and publishers to shame. Even though it isn't without it's flaws, Amid Evil is a ton of fun and does a lot of things right, and for the most part I've had a right blast. Most of all though, it's not only a good game, but it's one which feels remarkably fresh too.

Fans of Heretic and Hexen will instantly feel the inspirational vibes from those games here, but without a doubt Amid Evil draws from those games whilst also doing it's own thing too. I'm not one who really gets stoked by aesthetics, gameplay is king for me, but here everything feels SO unbelievably fresh, polished and unique that it's hard not to fall in love with them all. The music in particular is superb; this is definitely a game to play with headphones on.

But that's all backed up by great gameplay too anyway. Everything feels on-point, and the enemies come with some fantastically crafted attack patterns which force you to stay on your toes. It's fast, snappy fun which flows great. Feeding into that is the fact that each weapon remains relevant throughout the game, and that they are all useful against different types of enemies. A lot of playtesting and effort has clearly gone into this game, and it boy does it feel well balanced for it. I also don't think it's that easy either past the earlier stages; I died a shed load in the Forges! lol, and it didn't take much of a slip up to end up dead there. So, whilst it does start very easy, kudos on the overall difficulty curve.

The stage design is mostly positive too, with thematically lush stages crafted excellently to offer a nice blend of action, puzzles and secrets. None of the puzzles will tax you for long at all, this is nowhere near as complex as games such as Hexen 2, but they serve their purpose and the devs get very creative with some stages, throwing a lot of verticality into the mix. At it's best Amid Evil feels like a real adventure which isn't tight with it's "whoa!" moments either.

What does hinder the game though is it's pacing. Whilst the game's elements themselves are excellent, sometimes they are portioned unevenly and it can make the journey a bumpy one. Some stages are tipped far too much either way with their balance of action, puzzling or platforming. Like I say, those elements themselves are still all executed well, so in isolation they aren't an issue, but there were definitely stages were I was thinking "I've had enough platforming/puzzling here now, give me some action" and visa versa, but then said stage carried on with the same approach which it had already been throwing at me for 10-20 minutes previous.

To extend on that, I'd also say that a few stages just felt a bit too long; each world is broken up into 4 stages, and some of the latter stages probably could do with being sliced up slightly to form a 6-stage setup instead IMO. It's taking me over a month to grind out the last few stages and is starting to drag, simply because I knew I was having to find a 45-60 minute slot of the day to run through a stage, and for Popamole action that's just not a good portion size IMO. I know that'll reduce significantly as I master the stages, but honestly most stages past the half way mark should have been reduced by 20-30% to offer more bite-sized portions - Popamole games being portioned like adventure/RPG games is a real display of modern dev naivety. 

Also, and this is probably just a me thing, but I really wish there just wasn't any mana in this game, or at the very least some item which makes it irrelevant after the early stages. The endless cycle of loose mana...hunt mana...loose mana...hunt mana just grows tiresome, and there's no real need for mana here either as the enemies prompt you to change up weapons anyway (so the drive to switch weapons doesn't come from being mana-dry). I really hope any potential sequel ditches the mana angle, gives the game secrets which give you special items or player upgrades instead, and maybe even introduces Hexen 2 style characters.

Final minor gripe is that there are sections which are obviously there just to prompt you to activate "overdrive" mode. It just feels a bit cheap. "Overdrive" is way too readily available throughout the whole game anyway, and personally I think they should have made items which make this mode the core focus for exploration rather than mana, and restricted it to a far rarer event. Make a big deal of it next time! Feed the power-trip!

But these are minor gripes with what is otherwise a great blast.

8/10

Do you wish Quake had remained entirely fantasy as the original design hinted at? Are you sad because Heretic 2 can't be bought anywhere because of stupid rights disputes? Did you just absolutely hate Hexen's 'puzzles'? Let Amid Evil soothe your aches and drench you in the blood of your enemies.

Amid Evil is an FPS developed by Indefatigable, a company founded by a pair of good old boys whose careers have spanned decades, from Doom mods to the Rise of the Triad remake. It was also published by New Blood Interactive, who are quickly climbing my (short) list of favourite publishers together with Devolver. In the game you take on the role of the Champion, wielder of the Axe of the Black Labyrinth, as he cleanses several worlds of the influence of a mysterious Evil Force.

Graphically speaking, the game uses Unreal Engine 4 for a bunch of fancy lighting and particles but otherwise strains to stick to a retro-styled 'early 3D' look and succeeds beautifully in this goal. The old texturework is augmented by UE4's capabilities and as a result everything looks crisp, strange yet familiar. And since we're on the technical subject, the sound design and especially music are well done, courtesy of the ubiquitous Andrew Hulshult. Sure, it might feel a little odd to look at at first, but you get used to it pretty quickly.

Off to gameplay. Amid Evil borrows many elements from such classics as Unreal, Quake and especially Raven Software's first real debut, Heretic. Your ranged weapons are all magical staves or other such implements, the Champion laughs menacingly when he picks up a weapon, and fortunately your melee weapon doesn't suck. When swung, the Axe has a slight magnetic effect that attracts enemies into its swings and does considerable damage, enough to make short work of most enemies in a few swings. The ranged weapons are all quite different and use four colours of mana (ammunition) which you find scattered in levels along with health pickups and occasional powerups. Your rocket launcher equivalent is a staff that [i]pulls random planets from space and launches them at your enemies[/i]. And on top of all this, every weapon has an alternate (and much more powerful) firing mode which it uses when you're in Soul Mode, which you don't enter by using Tomes of Power, but by collecting souls off of dead enemies and filling a bar. For just one example, the Axe [i]will spin rapidly like a propeller in front of you. That's not how Axes should work[/i]. 

With all of these weapons, you have a great many levels to use them in. Your objective is to go through several worlds with four sprawling levels each, get to the exit of each level and destroy the boss monster of every episode before returning back to the hub world. Level and enemy design is (almost) completely different for every world, with the difficulty curve of the game progressing in both ways, from fighting evil mages in ancient temples to unknowable horrors in non-Euclidean fever dreams. All of these levels, enemies and more are described succinctly in your Codex, which helps add a touch of worldbuilding and even lore (even though there are numerous spelling mistakes that couldn't help but steal my eyes, but they can be forgiven). Speaking of levels, the bosses of each episode are challenging, impressive to behold and (except for one) not gimmicky in any way, but real tests for the Champion.

In conclusion, while I would (for whatever reason) still rank it below DUSK, Amid Evil is a fine shooter, well worth your time whether you're an old guard or fresh on the scene. Doubly so if you're tired of modernity and guns and would like a bit of fantasy added to the mix.

If you're anything like me, and love strange and unique fantasy settings, oh boy will you be drowning in just that. This is such an alien and fascinating world that I wish I could learn more about it beyond what the in-game lore blurbs give you. You'll notice enemies wielding weapons similar to the ones you do, like the Whisper's Edge or Star of Torment, but they're just something a little off or different that implies so much. Not to mention the environments that leave me postulating just what they may have looked like before "The Evil" spread its influence. Oh yeah, and the main antagonist being the pure embodiment of straight up "Evil" is delightfully simple and fun! There is not a single traditional fantasy creature to be seen, no elves or dwarves, everything is unique to itself (besides the literal dragon in the DLC, but like... c'mon). Not that I dislike traditional fantasy creatures/races, far from it! It's just so inspiring to see something so fresh and unique, it almost reminds me of the Dark Crystal in that way. And that is some insanely high praise coming from me.

There are also plenty of cool trippy visuals, especially in the last section of the base game. You can play most of the worlds/chapters in whatever order you want, though I personally would save Arcane Expanse (aka, the best chapter) for last before you enter the true final world. Every world has its own unique set of enemies, which incredibly aren't just reskins of previous enemies (except for a few enemies in Astral Equinox and Solar Solstice which are pretty similar, but that's literally the joke, and a good one at that). It always manages to refresh itself, which on a first play through is definitely impressive. A lot of them are variations on "dude in sick ass armor", but I love dudes in sick ass armor so that's a compliment. The colors and lighting are gorgeous, which build onto the excellent environmental design to really give an incredible aesthetic that is unique to each world, but consistent as a full product.

Basically, its a very good game. I'd love a sequel, but honestly anything that builds upon what they did here would be incredibly satisfying and I'd be eager to play! Buy this game and its DLC if you have any interest in "Boomer Shooters"! If you are disappointed something is wrong with you!

It's a good game, no more, no less. It is not some kind of revelation that would revolutionize the genre. It has its flaws, but nothing glaring. It does not tries to shoot above its station, only to miss and fall flat on its face. It does a thing, and does it well - a throwback to 90s shooters, no strings attached, no attempts to "modernize" the experience, no looter shooter mechanics, no procedural generation, here's some enemies and buttons, shoot one and press the other.

Artstyle is hard to describe, and it looks like it would be a massive eyesore - yet somehow it isn't. Levels are great. Each episode is distinct, and level designers used every trick in the book to avoid boring rectangles. Capabilities of a modern engine are also used to great extent - platform will never just move into place if it can sommersault on its way instead, bridges will reform out of broken fragments instead of just sliding out of the wall. Design-wise it is definitely an id school - you won't find realistic, lived-in interiors like in a Build game, levels are just vague abstract ideas of a castle or a temple [spoiler]unless it's episode 7, which is not abstract, but straight up surreal[/spoiler], but they look gorgeous, they flow well and they are just fun to play.

Gameplay-wise, it is closer to original Quake, with lots of jumping, rather low ammo stock, and enemies are small in numbers and tend to be on beefier side. Weapons are well made, they are distinct, have fun mechanics to them and all of them are useful, save maybe for the Whisper's Edge and default axe (it's not bad, but I rarely got a good opportunity to use it). Each episode has a separate enemy roster, so they can throw a curveball at you while you are still getting used to the new faces. Overall, I'd say the game is rather easy - I played it on Hard and never felt too overwhelmed. I also foolishly turned the automatic Soul mode off - bad idea, it makes you too skittish with soul modes, and it also makes it extremely easy to cheese the bosses. If you played Quake 2 to the end, you know what I'm talking about.

Amid Evil is the kind of game that reminds you why you fell in love with shooters in the first place. It doesn’t just borrow from the classics, it understands them, refines them, and unleashes something that feels both nostalgic and completely fresh.

Its roots in Hexen and Heretic are obvious in the best way: magical weapons, labyrinthine levels, and that distinct blend of fantasy and first-person carnage. But it never feels stuck in the past. Instead, it takes that foundation and builds something faster, smoother, and far more expressive. Combat is fluid and aggressive, with weapons that feel incredible to use, especially when powered up into their devastating alt forms.

The level design is where it really shines. Each episode feels like its own strange dimension, packed with verticality, secrets, and arenas that encourage movement and experimentation. There’s a constant sense of flow, of pushing forward through beautifully bizarre spaces that feel handcrafted for chaos.

And then there’s the atmosphere; abstract, surreal, and unforgettable. Glowing geometry, impossible structures, and cosmic vistas give the game a dreamlike quality that sets it apart from anything else in the genre.

New Blood clearly poured passion into every detail. This isn’t just a throwback, it’s a statement. It proves that the spirit of classic shooters is alive and evolving, and Amid Evil stands as one of the best modern examples of how to do it right.

[h1]The gist of it:[/h1]
AMID EVIL is yet another retro first-person shooter from the creators of Dusk, offering 10 hours of fun shooting though sadly not as interesting or exciting as you might expect. 

👍 [u]The good parts:[/u]
+Overall gunplay or in this case magic-wand play is fun.
+Locations are unique and interesting. 
+Graphical effects are very pretty.

👎[u]The bad parts:[/u]
-The story or lore, in this case, was kinda boring. 
-Pixelated textures really do not fit with the overall modern look of the game's graphics. 
-Weak boss fights. 

[h1]Story[/h1]
There isn't much of a story or even an atmospheric type of storytelling like Dusk has and the game pretty much explains everything in its main menu codex which I thought was kinda stupid. 

What made Dusk interesting is that it told a story through levels and the players imagination not forcing you to read the entire story in the main menu. AMID EVIL slaps you a lore where you're basically a chosen one that has to clear 7 major zones each governed by a God I think that were corrupted by some evil entity. That is pretty much it. 

There are some texts scattered around the levels but honestly, they do not tell much. Don't go in the game expecting something interesting or twisted. It was kinda boring, to be honest.

Story rating: 6/10

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The gameplay aspect of the game involves 6 types of magic wands if you can call them that and 1 melee weapon, that each has its own unique property or type of mana. There are 4 types of colored mana, orange, blue, green and purple, and 2 weapons for each type of mana with the exception of the purple and orange which have only one weapon.

They are quite nicely designed, from shooting random planets out of your wand to shooting electricity. Each weapon also has a powered mode, making them even more powerful as long as your soul mode or powered on mode lasts. 

Not much else can be said about the gameplay besides that all you're going to do is traverse multiple intricate levels filled with unique monsters and some platforming. Your arsenal will be tested significantly as you progress deeper in the game and the monsters get tougher. 

They are certainly not the most amazing types of weapons I've played but they do a good job of keeping things fun up until the end. Sadly the boss fights just like in Dusk are kinda underwhelming. I pretty much used soul mode and spammed the most powerful weapon and that was it. Some bosses may require some strategy before shooting them but nothing too advanced or hard to achieve. 

Gameplay rating: 8.5/10

[h1]Audio[/h1]
There's only a person talking in the game, the being that guides you or congratulates you but nothing else.

 Sound effects are not that interesting to discuss, they're all pretty much standard with no negatives. 

The soundtrack was supposed to be a good part of the game but as I progressed in the game I started noticing it less and less. It is way too atmospheric for this particular genre and on rare occasions where it does change the tempo to something more action-oriented, it ends too fast. Don't get me wrong, it's well crafted and atmospheric but honestly, I did not find it amazing as I hoped.

Audio rating:  8/10

[h1]Graphics, performance and tech analysis[/h1]
Now regarding the graphical part of the game, it's certainly a looker. Just like Dusk it brings us a sorta retro-pixelated style but with modern effects which can look odd, at least to me. I'm bored with pixelated indies so this is certainly a minus on my part but the overall atmosphere and how the lighting and special effects look, it certainly is fantastic.

Regarding performance and bugs, there were no issues at all and the game runs incredibly well.

Graphics, performance and tech analysis score: 8.5/10

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
AMID EVIL is certainly a competent shooter that offers a more unique set of weapons than we're normally used to while at the same time feeling familiar and with a nice atmosphere, the game overall gets my recommendation on any price. Amid Evil is a fast-paced, pixelated acid trip laced with gratuitous wizard murder. The atmosphere is like a Jack Kirby sci-fi illustration, projected on a four-dimensional object under a blacklight. And that's not even mentioning that Andrew Hulshult's soundtrack goes hard and never stops. 

Like the best boom shoots, it finds complexity in its simple gameplay. Each weapon has a function and a purpose. They are unique tools for turning Evil into a fine red mist. As a result, most of the fun comes from learning what weapons are effective in certain circumstances and swapping them out to optimize your gibbitute output. It's a lot like modern DOOM in that respect. No weapon is wasted, no overcharge is useless, no crystal wizard is left un-exploded by a projectile plant. Even The Axe of the Black Labyrinth plays a heavy role in higher difficulties. 

Every level is unique, carrying its own set of enemies. Most of them are slight re-skins (especially the flying enemies), but they bring enough of a unique twist to every setting. Sometimes, you'll lean heavily on the staff that shoots planets; other times, you'll use your lighting trident to exploit its chain-lighting effect on large groups of enemies. Bossfights are creative and sometimes take place in antigravity orbs.

There is some annoying platforming in later levels. But if some weird jumps are enough to ruin a game for you, you probably don't like shooters. I grew up on Turok, so it barely phases me. But besides that, every level is a slam dunk. It does a great job of telegraphing where to go and how to get to your objectives. I never felt like I was wandering in circles, wishing for a top-down map like I'm on an Apple II or something. 

Amid Evil excels beyond its inspiration, creating an identity as the perfect example of how to stick it to the AAA industry. There is no leveling, crafting, gimmicks, or expository cutscenes. This is a video game in the purest sense. You boot it up and kick ass right out of the gate. That's about as clean and straightforward as you can get. 

I hope they make another one—or at least a level editor—so I can keep making Amid Evil until this mid-life crisis runs its course.

There is a lot to be said about Amid Evil. I began supporting and playing through this wonderful game over a year ago and I loved the game more and more as it was closer to completion.

The premise of Amid Evil is good versus evil in a '90s FPS design style, many influences such as Wolfenstein 3D, DooM, Heretic, HeXen, and Quake. However, it is most like Heretic and HeXen, even though it has these strong influences, Amid Evil maintains an identity of its own with a crazy arsenal, unique foes, spectacular environments, and awesome music (by Andrew Hulshult). The weapons have a similar archetype as most FPS' of the past. The Axe of the Black Labyrinth, Staff of the Azure Orb, Whisper's Edge, Voltride, Celestial Claw, Staff of Torment, and the Aeturnum. Each have their own uses, for example the Axe can kill certain enemies in one hit that might take several shots from the Whisper's Edge or Voltride. The Celestial Claw launches different planets and even the Sun, acting like a rocket launcher. Aside from that, the enemies react differently to each weapon and have weaknesses and strengths to each.

Nextly, the level design is ludicrous, each one having a unique theme, similar to some other games we know and love. The first episode is more of a Medieval theme, the second being still somewhat Medieval, but with alien parasite type enemies. The third episode is like Mayan and Aztec atmosphere. The fourth being focused around the Sun and the fifth based on somewhat Dwarven designs. The sixth and seventh take on insane and very non-linear and arcane designs (hense the names Arcane Expanse and The Abyss). Furthermore, what makes each so unique and likable is the music, which is one of my favorite parts of the game.

Lastly, what made this game so enjoyable was the level of understanding from the devs and how they shaped the game from the influences of the past as well as the input of all of the people that stayed by the game in Early Access. I played from the beginning each time a new episode came out and gave a lot of feedback and created a guide to help make this the best experience possible. I hope they continue to support the game and possibly start new projects in the future that are on par with Amid Evil. Definitely one of the best games I have played in a while and have been dying to review it, just had to wait until it released. I recommend this game at full price as it is definitely worth it and it is worth it even more if it is on sale.

Pros:

- Most all enemies have unique death sounds and animations depending on how they're killed
- The majority of Amid Evil's weapons are projectile based, coupled with medium sized arenas lends itself to fast and frantic combat (reminiscent of OG Quake)
- The art-style is an interesting combination of super detailed sprite-work (yes, the weapons are sprites) and 3d modeling that somehow blend together seamlessly
- Speaking of art, the use of lighting in this game is just staggering. It won't even take you until the second level of the game to notice how amazing it looks seeing colored projectiles gliding softly through fog (most modern games don't even do this)
- Enemies are unique in their attack patterns and show off some pretty decent path finding, able to jump up to higher platforms or across chasms to get closer/a better vantage point on the player (sometimes they get stuck behind decorations in the environment but not often enough to be annoying)
- Every level has an amazing dynamic soundtrack composed by Andrew Hulshult which fits the mood perfectly
- Episode(s) 1, 2, 4, 6, and 7
- Seriously though, if for no other reason buy this game for Solar Solstice (episode 4) and Arcane Expanse (episode 6). The other episodes are good but these are better. Not only do they have some of the coolest visuals the game has to offer but they're easily the most challenging with some agile, hard-hitting opponents that will ruin you if you're not careful. In my opinion, Arcane Expanse edges out Solar Solsice just because of the level design as well as the amount of different enemy types you'll encounter.

Cons:
- Episode 3 and 5
- To be fair, The Sacred Path (episode 3) isn't as bad as it was in early access because they actually added enemy variety to it but it's still boring from a gameplay perspective due to the level layout. The first level has really narrow walkways and spawns rock golems in front of you (have to wait for spawning animation to finish before you can one-shot them with the celestial claw) and the level in general is very claustrophobic, making distancing yourself from enemies harder than it should be (especially on Evil difficulty). Secret hunting is especially annoying in the third level of this episode since it often requires you to drop down to a lower point you've already cleared of enemies to obtain secret items and you have to climb all the way back up without fighting anything. - The Forges (episode 5) on the other hand is just bad. Again the art and music are of really high standards and the first level lures you into thinking it's not going to be that bad because that incredible fog from Astral Equinox (episode 1) makes a return but looks and sound is pretty much all this episode has going for it. The levels are even more claustrophobic than the first level of episode 3 was and feature really annoying traps over pits of what I guess is lava and the enemies have some of the most annoying attacks I've ever seen in a game and in my opinion have way too much health. The roller ball enemies suck on Evil difficulty as they're able to catch up and outrun the player and just suck in general, have way too much health. Rock golems from episode 3 make a return with the same invulnerability on spawn mechanic but now they shoot lasers! Those floating mechanical testicle bastards shoot horizontal saw-blades at you while on tiny ledges over floors of lava. Ooh, the grappling hook guys... Bullet/shard spongy fools that predict shot where you're going and if that hook so much as looks at you the wrong way you'll be pulled across the map to wherever he is (usually over lava so if you kill him in mid flight you'll still take damage) and I have no idea how much damage his melee attack does but it's usually enough to kill me in one hit.
